issues.item: Triggers: Victim Similarity: People who look similar to the victims
issues.explanation: For a single-patient assault trauma, 'people who look similar to the victims' is clinically incoherent because it implies multiple victims or identification with other victims rather than the patient's own assault experience. A more self-referential trigger would be expected.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening
issues.explanation: 'Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening' sits awkwardly with the rest of the profile's self-directed shame and identity-change appraisals. It implies confidence that another person would have prevented the assault, which conflicts with the patient's own vulnerability/self-blame framing in a way that is hard to integrate clinically.

issues.item: Triggers: Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
issues.explanation: For an assault trauma in a 70-year-old male, 'medical procedures' plus 'body shame' implies a strong bodily injury/medical aftermath theme, but the rest of the profile does not support that theme. With only offender cues and intrusive thoughts otherwise present, the medical trigger looks insufficiently anchored and may be mismatched to the rest of the assault profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: 'Body shame' is not impossible after assault, but alongside 'defective self' and 'unrecognisable self' it suggests a bodily violation/injury-focused appraisal pattern that is not well reflected in the other selected nodes. The triggers and strategies mainly reflect avoidance, numbing, and offender-related activation rather than body-focused trauma processing.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Catastrophising Others: I worry obsessively about bad things happening to people I care about
issues.explanation: 'Catastrophising others' is weakly connected to the rest of the selected profile. The active formulation links Triggers strongly with Maladaptive Strategies and Negative Appraisals strongly with Triggers, but this strategy is not a plausible direct response to the chosen triggers (medical procedures, intrusive thoughts, offender cues) and is not well explained by the selected appraisals. It addresses a generalized harm concern that is otherwise absent from the profile.

vignette: Arthur Vance had spent three decades in commercial sales, a career that demanded steady handshakes, reliable smiles, and the quiet confidence of a man who could navigate unfamiliar cities with ease. The night everything changed, he had pulled his sedan into the dimly lit service lot behind a downtown hotel, exhausted from a long drive and looking forward to a quiet evening with his wife, Eleanor. He was alone in the car when three men approached the driver's side. There was no warning, only the sudden pressure of hands on his shoulders, the scrape of his seatbelt against his chest, and a face inches from his window, breathing heavily with the sharp, sour tang of whiskey. The assault lasted less than two minutes, but the combination of the face, the aggressive posture, and that particular alcohol smell seared itself into his attention. In the days that followed, the memory did not fade into a distant report; it arrived unbidden. Unwanted thoughts would surface while he was signing invoices or waiting for a conference call to connect, sudden and vivid, replaying the moment his keys clattered to the floor. Arthur quickly learned to navigate around the service lot, taking deliberate detours through three different cross streets so he would never pass within half a mile of where it happened. Avoid Location became a fixed habit, carved into his weekly travel patterns. At the same time, he began a constant, exhausting mental routine. When the memories pressed close, he told himself he had to keep his composure, so he forced his attention onto the dashboard, onto the rhythm of his windshield wipers, onto anything that would keep his mind from drifting back to the event. He tried hard not think about the trauma, treating every recollection like a draft he could close by sheer will. Alongside this mental effort, the quiet withdrawal he showed at work continued to unfold. Business dinners, once the backbone of his sales territory, suddenly felt heavy. When a client's drink clinked against a glass or a waiter passed carrying a tray of amber bottles, the alcohol smell would rise in the air, and Arthur's chest would tighten. He would abruptly excuse himself, claiming a tight deadline, and leave the venue. His wife noticed the sudden absences, but Arthur offered no explanation, only a steady, unchanging distance from their shared routines. Over the months, the distance hardened into something deeper. Arthur found himself sitting in his study, staring at the grain of his desk, unable to feel the frustration or the sorrow that had once moved him. I numb my feelings, he would think, treating emotional withdrawal as a necessary shield. Alongside the numbing, the quiet, persistent weight remained. Arthur began to look at his reflection and feel a strange disconnection. The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, he told Eleanor one evening when she asked why he no longer laughed at their old comedies or wanted to take long walks. He stopped seeing the assertive, well-connected salesman he used to be. Instead, he saw a man who had frozen, a man who had made a split-second decision to hand over his wallet without a word, and in the silence of his own kitchen, he convinced himself that the event happened because of the way I acted. There was a gap in his courage, a flaw in his judgment, and he had come to believe there is something wrong with me as a person, a defect that made him vulnerable to men who knew how to strike when they thought no one was watching. For over forty years, Arthur had managed the weight of it by staying busy, by keeping his territory full, by treating his life as a series of transactions that required steady hands and a clear head. But at seventy, the old detours and the quiet suppression began to fray. Eleanor's gentle insistence that he see a therapist had finally crossed a threshold. He had come to the clinic on a Tuesday morning, his sales portfolio folded neatly in his lap, more afraid of the flat, untroubled life he was settling into than of the memories themselves. He wanted to understand how the man he was had become the man he was no longer, and he hoped, quietly, that someone could help him remember how to feel without the floor giving way beneath him.
